questions.q: Why does this lesson treat NPSP's donor/gift model and PMM's program-delivery model as two different data models, even though both can reference the same Contact?
options: Because PMM replaces NPSP entirely and the two cannot coexist
Because NPSP cannot track Contacts at all
Because they answer two different questions — who gave what and when, versus who received what service and whether it was delivered
Because donors and program clients can never be the same person
questions.explain: NPSP's model is shaped around fundraising (who gave what, when, will they give again); PMM's model is shaped around service delivery (who received what, in what engagement, with what outcome) — genuinely different questions, even when the same real person shows up in both.

questions.q: Why can't Harlow's tutoring cohort be adequately represented by a plain one-record-per-child case model with no group structure?
options: Because cohorts are only relevant to food-assistance programs, not tutoring
Because case models cannot store a child's name
Because PMM does not support any individual-level tracking at all

Because nothing in that model links an individual child's attendance to the cohort's overall session, which a Program Engagement and Service Delivery are specifically built to represent at both levels
questions.explain: A one-to-one case model has no way to represent group-level participation alongside individual attendance. Program Engagements and Service Deliveries are designed to represent both the cohort's session and each child's own history within it.

questions.q: What practical benefit does this lesson name from PMM sitting on top of NPSP's existing Contact/Account model rather than creating a separate set of "program people"?
options: It lets Harlow see when the same real person is both a donor and a client, avoiding double-counting in impact reporting
It removes the need for any Account records at all
It means program staff can see a client's full donation history by default, regardless of consent
It eliminates the need for Service Delivery records
questions.explain: Because PMM extends NPSP's existing people model instead of duplicating it, Harlow can recognize when a tutoring parent or a scholarship recipient's relative is also a donor or volunteer — important for honest, non-duplicated impact numbers.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend a phased rollout (tutoring, then food assistance, then scholarships) over building all three programs simultaneously?
options: Because Salesforce technically limits an org to one active program at a time
Because each program has its own service-delivery shape, and launching all three at once means debugging three new configurations and workflows with no working example to learn from first
Because the executive director explicitly banned simultaneous rollouts
Because PMM cannot be installed more than once per org
questions.explain: Each program's service-delivery pattern (cohort sessions vs. one-time handouts vs. annual renewal checks) is different enough that building all three at once multiplies risk with no earlier phase's lessons to draw on — a scoped, phased rollout lets each phase inform the next.

questions.q: What two PMM objects does this lesson name as extending NPSP specifically to track program participation and individual instances of service?
options: Opportunities and Campaigns
Household Accounts and Recurring Donations
Program Engagements and Service Deliveries
Leads and Cases
questions.explain: Program Engagements track a person's or cohort's participation in a program, and Service Deliveries track each specific instance of service rendered against that engagement — the two objects PMM adds on top of NPSP's donor-focused model.
